title: Conjecture 4 (Sumner's Conjecture)
statement_text: Every oriented tree of order $n>1$ is $(2n-2)$-unavoidable.
context_text: Sumner's conjecture is a celebrated open problem in the area of unavoidability of oriented trees in tournaments. It would be tight, as the out-star $S^+_n$ is not contained in the regular tournaments of order $2n-3$. The best known upper bound prior to this paper was proved by Dross and Havet using median orders.
paper_contribution: The paper generalizes linear unavoidability of oriented trees to $k$-blow-ups (proving $(2^{10+18k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidability) and $k$-extensions (proving $(2\cdot 3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}\cdot|V(F)|)$-unavoidability), but does not directly improve the $(2n-2)$ bound in Sumner's conjecture.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Problem 6
statement_text: Let $\alpha$ be a positive real number. Does there exist a polynomial $P_{\alpha}$ such that $\operatorname{unvd}(D)\leqslant P_{\alpha}(|V(D)|)$ for every digraph with maximum average degree at most $\alpha$?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. Bucić, Letzter and Sudakov asked whether acyclic digraphs of bounded maximum average degree are linearly unavoidable. Draganić et al. proved this for $k$-th powers of directed paths, but Fox, He and Wigderson showed it fails in general: for every $\Delta\ge2$ and large $n$ there is an acyclic digraph with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\ge n^{\Omega(\Delta^{2/3}/\log^{5/3}\Delta)}$. This problem asks whether polynomial unavoidability still holds (the digraphs are implicitly acyclic). The companion question is which families of bounded maximum average degree are linearly unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: If $\cal F$ is linearly unavoidable and has bounded maximum average degree, then ${\cal F}[k]$ is also linearly unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. The $k$-blow-up $D[k]$ of $D$ replaces each vertex by an independent set of $k$ vertices, with arcs from the copies of $u$ to the copies of $v$ for every arc $uv$ of $D$ (the paper's formal definition additionally restricts these arcs to pairs of copies with distinct indices), and $\mathcal{F}[k]=\{D[k]:D\in\mathcal{F}\}$. The bounded maximum average degree condition is necessary: the disjoint union of a transitive tournament of order $\lfloor\log n\rfloor+1$ and isolated vertices is $n$-unavoidable, but its $k$-blow-up has maximum average degree $k\lfloor\log n\rfloor$, hence unavoidability at least about $n^{k/2}/2$. The conjecture holds for directed paths (by the result of Draganić et al. on powers of directed paths), and the authors prove it for oriented trees and forests: the $k$-blow-up of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $(2^{10+18k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Problem 8
statement_text: What is the infimum of all the constants $C$ such that for every large enough integer $n$, the $k$-blow-up of every oriented tree of order $n$ is $(C^{k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidable?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. The $k$-blow-up $D[k]$ of $D$ replaces each vertex by an independent set of $k$ vertices, with arcs from the copies of $u$ to the copies of $v$ for every arc $uv$ of $D$ (the paper's formal definition additionally restricts these arcs to pairs of copies with distinct indices), and $\mathcal{F}[k]=\{D[k]:D\in\mathcal{F}\}$. An oriented tree is an orientation of a tree. The authors prove that the $k$-blow-up of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $(2^{10+18k}\cdot kn)$-unavoidable, which is certainly not tight. Since the $k$-blow-up of a tree of order $n$ has maximum average degree $2k-2k/n$, the lower bound $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$ shows that the optimal bound is of the form $2^{\Theta(k)}\cdot kn$; the problem asks for the optimal base $C$.

title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: There exists a constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{unvd}(D)\leqslant C\cdot\operatorname{unvd}(D-v)$ for every acyclic digraph $D$ and for every vertex $v$ of $D$.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. Sumner's conjecture states that every oriented tree of order $n>1$ is $(2n-2)$-unavoidable; it is known for large $n$, and Häggkvist and Thomason proved that oriented trees are linearly unavoidable. For a source or sink $x$ of an acyclic digraph $D$, a simple induction argument gives $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le2\,\mathrm{unvd}(D-x)$, which yields the Erdős–Moser bound $2^{n-1}$. The conjecture asserts that deleting an arbitrary vertex can only decrease the unavoidability by a constant factor. Together with Sumner's conjecture it would imply that every $k$-extension of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $C^k(2n-2)$-unavoidable (an acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices), and more generally that $k$-extensions of a linearly unavoidable family are linearly unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every integer $k$, every $k$-extension of an oriented tree of order $n$ is $C^{k}(2n-2)$-unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. An acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices (the added vertices). Sumner's conjecture states that every oriented tree of order $n>1$ is $(2n-2)$-unavoidable; it is known for large $n$, and Häggkvist and Thomason proved that oriented trees are linearly unavoidable. The conjecture would follow from Sumner's conjecture together with the conjecture that there is a constant $C$ such that $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C\,\mathrm{unvd}(D-v)$ for every acyclic digraph $D$ and every vertex $v$ (true with $C=2$ when $v$ is a source or sink). The authors prove a weaker result: every $k$-extension of a sufficiently large oriented tree (or forest) $F$ is $(2\cdot3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}\cdot|V(F)|)$-unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: If $\cal F$ is linearly unavoidable, then the family of $k$-extensions of digraphs in $\cal F$ is also linearly unavoidable.
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. An acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices (the added vertices). This would follow from the conjecture that there is a constant $C$ such that $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C\,\mathrm{unvd}(D-v)$ for every acyclic digraph $D$ and every vertex $v$, since a $k$-extension adds $k$ vertices. The authors prove it for oriented trees and oriented forests: every $k$-extension of a sufficiently large oriented tree $F$ is $(2\cdot3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}\cdot|V(F)|)$-unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments

title: Problem 12
statement_text: What is the minimum function $f$ such that every $k$-extension of every forest of order $n$ is $(2^{f(k)}\cdot n)$-unavoidable?
context_text: A digraph $D$ is $p$-unavoidable if it is contained (as a subdigraph) in every tournament of order $p$, and its unavoidability $\mathrm{unvd}(D)$ is the smallest such $p$; it exists iff $D$ is acyclic, and every acyclic digraph of order $n$ is $2^{n-1}$-unavoidable (Erdős–Moser). A family $\mathcal{F}$ is linearly unavoidable if there is a constant $C$ with $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le C|V(D)|$ for all $D\in\mathcal{F}$, and polynomially unavoidable if $\mathrm{unvd}(D)\le P(|V(D)|)$ for some polynomial $P$. The maximum average degree of a digraph is the maximum average degree over its nonempty subdigraphs, and an acyclic digraph of maximum average degree $\alpha$ has $\mathrm{unvd}(D)>2^{\alpha/2}$. An acyclic digraph $D$ is a $k$-extension of $A$ if $D-S=A$ for some set $S$ of $k$ vertices (the added vertices). Forests here are oriented forests (orientations of forests, including arcless digraphs). The authors prove that every $k$-extension of a sufficiently large oriented forest $F$ is $(2\cdot3^{\binom{2k+2}{2}}|V(F)|)$-unavoidable, so $f(k)$ is at most quadratic in $k$, and they show that some $k$-extensions of the arcless digraph on $n$ vertices have unavoidability $2^kn-o(n)$, so $f$ is at least linear. The same question applies to subfamilies, starting with arcless digraphs. This is the analogue for extensions of the question on the optimal base $C$ such that $k$-blow-ups of oriented trees of order $n$ are $(C^k\cdot kn)$-unavoidable.
paper_title: Blow-ups and extensions of trees in tournaments
